title: Former NAFCO CEO, Wife Face 20 Criminal Charges Over Alleged GH¢54m Financial Improprieties
author: Bosomtwi-Web
excerpt: Fresh court documents filed at the High Court in Accra have slapped former National Food and Buffer Stock Company Chief Executive Officer, Hanan Abdul-Wahab Aludiba, and his wife, Faiza Seidu Wuni, with 20 criminal charges over alleged financial improprieties involving millions of Ghana cedis.
content:
The charge sheet, filed by the Office of the Attorney General and Ministry of Justice on May 15, 2026, accuses the couple of offences including stealing, defrauding by false pretences, wilfully causing financial loss to the State, abuse of public office for profit, dishonestly receiving, and money laundering.

The latest development follows the re-arrest of the former NAFCO boss and his wife by operatives of the Economic and Organised Crime Office shortly after they had been discharged by the High Court in an earlier matter.

According to court filings, prosecutors allege that Mr Aludiba fraudulently obtained GH¢734,400 — the cedi equivalent of US$127,500 — from NAFCO in 2017 under the guise of rent payments said to cover the period between May 2017 and May 2019.

The prosecution contends that the claim was false and amounted to defrauding by false pretence contrary to Section 131 of the Criminal Offences Act.

A separate charge accuses him of wilfully causing financial loss to the State through the same alleged rent arrangement.

The documents further allege that between February 2017 and February 2025, Mr Aludiba diverted approximately GH¢50.8 million from NAFCO through a private entity identified as Sawtina Enterprise, purportedly for the procurement of food supplies.

Prosecutors say the transactions amounted to stealing and abuse of public office for personal gain, resulting in substantial financial loss to the state agency.

In another set of allegations, the state claims the former CEO channelled NAFCO funds to a business allegedly owned by his wife, identified as Alqarni Enterprise.

Court documents allege that between September 2018 and August 2019, more than GH¢3.34 million was paid to the company for supposed food supply transactions that prosecutors describe as fraudulent.

Faiza Seidu Wuni, the second accused person, is facing additional charges of defrauding by false pretence, dishonestly receiving and money laundering.

According to prosecutors, she falsely represented that her company had supplied food items to NAFCO, causing the agency to release over GH¢3.34 million.

The state also alleges that she knowingly possessed funds believed to have been obtained unlawfully.

The money laundering charge, brought under the Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2020 (Act 1044), accuses her of allegedly taking possession of funds while aware they had been acquired through stealing.

The case has already attracted public and political attention following complaints by defence lawyers over the treatment of the accused persons after their re-arrest.

Lawyer for the former NAFCO CEO, Godfred Yeboah Dame, earlier criticised EOCO investigators, alleging that the accused persons were denied access to legal counsel and refused bail despite existing court processes and earlier bail conditions.

Mr Dame also described the prosecution’s conduct as an abuse of prosecutorial discretion and claimed his clients had suffered what he termed “pre-trial torture and harassment.”

NAFCO, a state-owned institution established to support food security and stabilise agricultural commodity prices in Ghana, has in recent years faced increased scrutiny over procurement systems, storage management and financial operations.

The matter is expected to return to court in the coming days as prosecutors move to formally prosecute the new charges against the accused persons.

title: More die of suspected Ebola as WHO warns that numbers will rise further
author: BBC
excerpt: The World Health Organization (WHO) says there have now been 600 suspected cases of Ebola and 139 suspected deaths, with numbers expected to rise further given the time taken to detect the virus.
content:
Fifty-one cases have now been confirmed in the Democratic Republic of Congo - where the first case was reported - and two in neighbouring Uganda, WHO chief Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Wednesday.

Speaking to journalists in Geneva, he said the outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of Ebola was likely to have started "a couple of months ago".

On Sunday, the WHO declared a public health emergency of international concern, but said it was not at pandemic level.

Ghebreyesus said that after meeting on Tuesday, the health organisation's emergency committee agreed the situation was "not a pandemic emergency".

"WHO assesses the risk of the epidemic as high at the national and regional levels and low at the global level," he explained.

The 51 cases confirmed in DR Congo are in its eastern Ituri province - the epicentre of the outbreak - and the North Kivu province. Of the two confirmed in Uganda's capital, Kampala, both had travelled from DR Congo, one of whom has died.

"We know the scale of the epidemic in DRC is much larger," the WHO chief said, adding that healthcare workers were among those who had died, which was a particular concern.

A WHO official said investigations were under way to find out how long the virus had been spreading for, but that their priority was to curb transmission.


The first known case was a nurse who developed symptoms and died on 24 April, in Ituri's provincial capital Bunia.

The body was repatriated to Mongwalu, one of two gold-mining towns where the majority of cases have been reported.

Four areas in Ituri have been affected by the outbreak: Mongwalu, Bunia, Rwampara and Nyakunde.

In North Kivu, rebel-controlled Goma, eastern DR Congo's biggest city and Butembo have reported cases.


DR Congo is facing its 17th outbreak of Ebola, but the Bundibugyo species - which has not been seen for more than a decade - brings its own difficulties.

Bundibugyo has only caused two previous outbreaks, when it killed about a third of those infected.

There is no approved vaccine for Bundibugyo, but experimental ones are in development. It is possible that a vaccine for another species, Zaire - which the country has dealt with on numerous occasions - may offer some protection.

There are also no drugs that target Bundibugyo, making it harder to treat.

Following criticism from the US on Tuesday that the WHO was "a little late" in identifying the outbreak, Ghebreyesus said these comments might have been caused by a lack of understanding.

"We should appreciate what was done so fast in a highly complex setting," the WHO said.

Initial symptoms of Ebola mirror illnesses such as malaria and typhoid, which are common in DR Congo.

Eastern DR Congo is also badly hit by years of conflict, bringing additional difficulties in dealing with the virus.

title: Bernard Antwi Boasiako has marked his 50th birthday with the donation of an ambulance to the Kuntanase Government Hospital.
author: Bosomtwi-web
excerpt: Chairman Wontumi marks his 50th birthday with the donation of an ambulance to Kuntanase Government Hospital
content:
Bernard Antwi Boasiako has marked his 50th birthday with the donation of an ambulance to the Kuntanase Government Hospital, in a move aimed at strengthening emergency healthcare services in the area.

https://www.facebook.com/share/r/18Q5EgRXK1/?mibextid=wwXIfr

The presentation, which formed part of activities to commemorate his milestone birthday, is expected to significantly improve the hospital’s capacity to respond to medical emergencies, particularly in surrounding communities where access to timely transportation to health facilities remains a challenge.

Speaking at the event, Chairman Wontumi emphasised the importance of supporting the health sector, noting that access to emergency care can be the difference between life and death. He indicated that the donation was his way of giving back to society and supporting efforts to improve healthcare delivery.

Health officials and community members welcomed the gesture, describing it as timely and impactful. They noted that the ambulance would help reduce delays in transporting critically ill patients and enhance referrals to larger medical facilities when necessary.

The donation also highlights the growing role of private individuals and political figures in supporting public healthcare infrastructure, particularly in underserved areas.

title: WAEC Relocates Ekumfi T.I Ahmadiyya SHS Candidates Over Alleged Exam Malpractice
author: Bosomtei-Web
excerpt: The West African Examinations Council has relocated candidates of Ekumfi T.I Ahmadiyya Senior High School to a different examination centre following allegations of examination malpractice involving two teachers of the school.
content:
In a letter dated May 17, 2026, and signed by the Cape Coast Branch Controller, Charles Henyo, WAEC directed the school’s headmaster to ensure that all candidates sit for their ongoing 2026 West African Senior School Certificate Examination at Mankessim Senior High Technical School.

According to WAEC, the decision followed the arrest of two teachers from the school who allegedly compromised the French 1 paper in the ongoing WASSCE for School Candidates.

“Following the arrest of two teachers from your school who compromised the French 1 paper in the ongoing WASSCE (SC), 2026, the Council can no longer trust the integrity of your school to conduct the examination devoid of malpractice,” the letter stated.

WAEC explained that the relocation serves as an interim measure while investigations and further reviews are conducted.

The examination body indicated that all examination papers scheduled between May 18 and May 22, 2026, would be written at Mankessim Senior High Technical School under fresh supervision and invigilation arrangements.

However, WAEC clarified that the Chemistry 3 Alternative A practical examination would still be conducted at the original premises of Ekumfi T.I Ahmadiyya SHS.

The Council further instructed the school authorities to arrange transportation for examination materials and supervisors between the WAEC depot and the new examination centre.

WAEC also directed the school to provide police escort services for the transportation and handling of examination materials during the exercise.

“You shall also make arrangement for the Police Escort on the rounds,” the statement added.

The Council stressed that strict compliance with the directives was necessary and indicated that additional instructions would be communicated after the ongoing review process.

title: Sod Cut for Construction of 24-Hour Model Market in Ejura
author: Bosomtwi Web
excerpt: Construction has officially begun on a new 24-hour model market project in the Ejura Municipality aimed at expanding economic opportunities and creating sustainable jobs for residents.
content:
The project forms part of President John Dramani Mahama’s ongoing “Resetting Agenda” and the government’s broader push to implement a 24-hour economy policy across the country.

The market is expected to include lockable stores, open stalls and several supporting facilities designed to sustain commercial activities around the clock.

Planned amenities include a police station, fire station, clinic, pharmacies, model school, restaurants, women’s bank, warehouse and other essential services.

The sod-cutting ceremony was led by the Ashanti Regional Minister, Frank Amoakohene, together with the Municipal Chief Executive for Ejura Sekyedumase, Rafiu Adams Seidu.

Dr Amoakohene described the initiative as part of government’s long-term vision to establish similar modern markets across districts nationwide to stimulate local economic growth and support the 24-hour economy agenda.

He expressed gratitude to President Mahama for what he described as a transformative initiative and also commended the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs for its role in driving the implementation process.

The Regional Minister further praised the collaborative efforts of the Member of Parliament for the area, Mohammed Bawah Bariamah, and the Municipal Chief Executive for contributing to development projects within the municipality.

### Call for Community Support

Dr Amoakohene appealed to chiefs and residents of the municipality to cooperate fully with contractors to ensure the timely completion of the project.

The MCE, Mr Seidu, stated that the Assembly, with support from traditional authorities and the MP, has undertaken several projects through the District Assembly Common Fund and other legacy initiatives.

According to him, these projects include the construction of five Community-based Health Planning and Services compounds, classroom blocks, public toilet facilities, refuse evacuation programmes and the drilling of 20 mechanised boreholes, many of which are at various stages of completion.

Chairing the event was the Chief of Ejura, Barima Osei Hwedie II, who commended the government, the MP and the MCE for their collaborative efforts toward the municipality’s development.

He noted that their commitment and hard work were already visible through the number of projects undertaken within a relatively short period.

The traditional ruler also pledged the support of the traditional council in providing land for future development projects within the Ejura Sekyedumase municipality.

title: Fifa ordered to explain World Cup ticket pricing
author: BBC Sports
excerpt: Fifa must answer questions after allegations of "artificially inflating prices" and "misleading fans" over the sale of tickets for the 2026 World Cup.
content:
It comes as the attorneys general of New York and New Jersey officially launched an investigation into Fifa's practices.

New Jersey attorney general Jennifer Davenport called the process a "gauntlet of confusion, fake scarcity and impossibly high prices".

She added there would be a "thorough investigation of Fifa's conduct" with world football's governing body subpoenaed to provide information.

A subpoena compels a party to release specified internal documents or information.

Davenport made a joint announcement alongside New York attorney general Letitia James and the New York City department of consumer and worker protection (DCWP).

DCWP commissioner Samuel AA Levine said the body would be taking "allegations of blatantly deceptive conduct very seriously" and would look into allegations of "artificially inflating prices".

Palladium

In particular, Fifa has been asked to explain why tickets have "exceeded the prices for any previous World Cup tournament".

Fans have reported they were "misled" about the location of seats, including through the creation of more expensive 'front' category tickets released after the initial sales.

It is also alleged variable pricing through various phases had allowed Fifa to raise prices for about 90 of the 104 fixtures by an average of 34%.

The investigation will consider how the ticket release schedule and public statements may have impacted prices.

Fifa has declined to comment.

'Not an invitation to exploit residents and visitors'
Fifa has regularly talked up the demand for tickets, with Fifa president Gianni Infantino defending the cost by saying they reflect the public's "absolutely crazy" appetite for the summer tournament.

But as of Wednesday, there were face-value tickets available for 86 of the 104 matches and all but 10 of the group-stage matches, for which the fixtures have long been known.

The attorneys general in particular highlighted the cost of tickets for eight matches, including the final, at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

"Being honest about ticket sales is not complicated," Davenport said. "It's an honour to host the World Cup but the event is not an invitation to exploit our residents and visitors."

James said local residents "deserve a fair shot at affordable tickets".

"No-one should be manipulated into paying sky-high prices for seats and fans should be able to trust that the tickets they purchase will be the ones they receive," James added.

Levine said supporters should expect "transparency and fairness" when buying tickets for the World Cup.

"Reports of Fifa conduct in violation of the city's consumer protection law, including misleading fans about seat locations and artificially inflating prices, are deeply troubling," Levine said.

The investigation comes after California attorney general Rob Bonta sent a letter to Fifa, external raising concerns about "potentially misleading ticketing practices" earlier this month.

Local organisers have been at loggerheads with Fifa for the past few months over high costs.

New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill previously criticised Fifa's refusal to subsidise transport at the event and insisted local taxpayers would not foot the bill.


After initially announcing a train ticket would cost $150 (£111), earlier this month NJ Transit backtracked and reduced the fare to $98 (£73).

Rail journeys from Penn Station in Manhattan to the venue - a distance of about 18 miles - are normally $12.90 (£9.50) for a return fare.

title: Minority MPs Resist Proposed Exemptions in Anti-LGBTQ Bill as Parliament Debates Scope of Law
author: Bosomtwi Web
excerpt: Parliament has witnessed fresh tensions over the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill, 2025, as co-sponsor John Ntim Fordjour and other Minority Members of Parliament push back against proposed exemptions for journalists, medical professionals, lawyers and other service providers.
content:
The disagreement arose during clause-by-clause consideration of provisions intended to protect certain professional activities from being interpreted as promotion or advocacy of LGBTQ-related issues.

The proposed amendments seek to exempt journalists and media organisations reporting on LGBTQ matters in the ordinary course of their work, as well as medical practitioners, counsellors, psychologists and lawyers offering professional services to individuals identified as LGBTQ persons.

However, the MP for Assin South, John Ntim Fordjour, together with the MP for Bosome-Freho, Nana Asafo-Adjei Ayeh, argued that the exemptions would dilute the intent of the legislation and create loopholes that could be exploited to advance LGBTQ advocacy.

Nana Asafo-Adjei Ayeh said the provisions significantly alter the original bill introduced in the previous Parliament, insisting that the new clauses go beyond what was previously approved by sponsors.

He argued that the exemptions for NGOs, academic work, medical research and journalism amount to a “watering down” of the bill’s core purpose.

Rev. Ntim Fordjour also rejected the inclusion of protections for medical, surgical, psychological and counselling services, stating that such provisions were not part of the original legislative proposal.

He further opposed exemptions related to media reporting and public health interventions, including HIV and AIDS-related programmes, warning that they could indirectly support LGBTQ activities.

According to him, sponsors of the bill would resist any attempt to incorporate such provisions, describing them as unacceptable amendments.

“I find it highly problematic, any attempt by this House to push any of these exceptions in. We will resist it,” he said.

However, Majority Leader Mahama Ayariga defended the proposed exemptions, arguing that they are intended to ensure that legitimate professional duties are not criminalised.

He maintained that the bill remains focused on prohibiting both LGBTQ practices and advocacy, and insisted that the clarifications would help prevent constitutional and legal challenges.

Mr. Ayariga added that it would be unreasonable for courts to support the prosecution of lawyers or journalists performing their professional responsibilities.

The debate over the bill continues to generate sharp divisions in Parliament as lawmakers consider the final shape of one of Ghana’s most contentious pieces of legislation.

Source: Myjoyonline

title: Cabinet Approves Major Decentralisation Reforms; Election of MMDCEs Proposed
author: Bosomtwi Web
excerpt: Cabinet has approved sweeping reforms to Ghana’s decentralisation system, paving the way for the direct election of Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs) and a comprehensive review of the country’s local governance framework.
content:
The reforms, outlined in the new National Decentralisation Policy and Strategic Framework (2026–2030), seek to deepen democratic governance, strengthen citizen participation and improve accountability at the local level.

Executive Secretary of the Inter-Ministerial Coordinating Committee on Decentralisation (IMCCoD), Dr Gameli Kewuribe Hoedoafia, disclosed that the current batch of MMDCEs appointed by John Dramani Mahama could be the last to assume office under the existing constitutional arrangement.

### Direct Election of MMDCEs

A key feature of the proposed reforms is the amendment of Article 243(1) of the 1992 Constitution, which currently grants the President the authority to appoint MMDCEs subject to approval by assembly members.

Under the proposed changes, district chief executives would be elected directly by the people through a non-partisan electoral process.

According to Dr. Hoedoafia, the government opted for a non-partisan system following extensive consultations, which revealed strong public support for electing MMDCEs while keeping local governance free from partisan political influence.

Constitutional amendment processes, including a referendum, are expected to take place between 2027 and 2029 to facilitate the transition.

### New Local Governance Law in the Works

As part of the reforms, the government is reviewing the Local Governance Act, 2016 (Act 936), with a new Local Governance Bill expected to be presented to Parliament before the end of 2026.

Dr. Hoedoafia explained that the review is necessary after nearly a decade of implementation exposed gaps and operational challenges within the existing legislation.

The Legislative Review Committee of IMCCoD is currently leading the process before the proposed bill is submitted to the Ministry of Local Government, Cabinet and subsequently Parliament.

### Integrated Planning Reforms

The proposed legislation will also introduce reforms aimed at improving planning and development coordination at the district level.

Dr. Hoedoafia said spatial planning and development planning functions, which are currently fragmented across different departments, would be integrated into a single planning framework to improve efficiency and address zoning, permitting and land-use challenges.

### Stronger Accountability Mechanisms

The reforms further seek to strengthen accountability by establishing local accountability platforms similar to Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee.

Under the proposal, MMDCEs and other public officials will be required to publicly account for the use of resources and implementation of development projects within their jurisdictions.

The policy also proposes stricter criteria for appointing the 30 percent government nominees to district assemblies to ensure the positions are occupied by individuals with relevant expertise rather than serving as avenues for political patronage.

### Increased District Assemblies Common Fund Allocation

In a move aimed at enhancing local development financing, the policy proposes increasing the constitutional minimum allocation to the District Assemblies Common Fund from five percent to 7.5 percent.

While some stakeholders have advocated for a 10 percent allocation, government officials say the proposed increase represents a gradual and sustainable approach to strengthening local governance and service delivery across the country.

The reforms are expected to significantly reshape Ghana’s decentralisation architecture and strengthen grassroots governance once the required constitutional and legislative processes are completed.

title: Manhyia Palace Partners UNESCO Ghana for 2026 Otumfuo Art Awards
author: bosomtwi-web
excerpt: The Manhyia Palace Museum has announced a landmark partnership with UNESCO Ghana ahead of the second edition of the Otumfuo Osei Tutu II Art Awards scheduled for May 13, 2026, in Kumasi.
content:
The collaboration is expected to boost efforts to promote Ghanaian visual arts on the international stage while preserving the country’s rich cultural and artistic heritage.

Speaking at a press briefing in Kumasi, the Director of the Manhyia Palace Museum, Ivor Agyeman-Duah, stated that the awards ceremony will be held at the Otumfuo Osei Tutu II Auditorium under the patronage of Otumfuo Osei Tutu II and Lady Julia Osei Tutu.

Organisers say the awards are aimed at recognising both established and emerging creative talents whose works continue to shape Ghana’s cultural identity through artistic innovation and excellence.

As part of activities leading to the main ceremony, a Laureates’ Dinner will be organised on May 12 to bring together artists, curators, cultural leaders and distinguished guests to celebrate excellence in visual arts and cultural preservation.

This year’s laureates were selected through an independent jury process involving Ghanaian and international experts in visual arts, art history and curation.

Among the eight honourees are internationally acclaimed contemporary artist Ibrahim Mahama, painters Victor Butler and Larry Otoo, portrait artist Afia Prempeh, and New York-based installation artist Yaw Owusu.

The list also includes curator Osei Bonsu, artist Julie Hudson, and Seychellois contemporary artist Leon Raddegonde.

Instituted in 2025, the Otumfuo Osei Tutu II Art Awards emerged following the successful return of royal regalia looted from the Manhyia Palace during the Anglo-Asante Wars.

Organisers explained that the subsequent “Homecoming” exhibition inspired the establishment of the awards scheme as a long-term initiative dedicated to safeguarding Ghana’s artistic and cultural heritage.

The awards honour excellence in painting, sculpture, traditional goldsmithing, installation art, art history and distinguished curation, with recipients selected based on originality, authenticity, cultural impact and contribution to Ghanaian creativity.

title: AsanteheneAt27: Lady Julia Celebrates Otumfuo
author: Story by Hajara Fuseini@opemsuo
excerpt: Lady Julia Osei Tutu has paid tribute to her royal spouse on the occasion of his 27th enstoolment anniversary.
content:
Her Royal Highness led tributes to the King, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, as Asanteman converged at Dwabrem, Manhyia Palace, to celebrate 27 years of distinguished service and local and global impact.Museums

Accompanied by an entourage, Lady Julia proceeded to the seat of His Majesty to pay homage, congratulate her husband, and extend goodwill on behalf of the royal household.

Her tribute reflected not only a wife’s admiration but also Asanteman’s collective gratitude for a reign defined by cultural preservation, development, and diplomacy. Today’s Akwasidae
For the first time in 27 years, the 16th Occupant of the Golden Stool, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, marked his enstoolment anniversary on Akwasidae, the sacred festival of the Asante Kingdom.This year, April 26 — the exact date His Majesty ascended the Golden Stool in 1999 — falls on the 3rd Akwasidae of 2026, creating a historic overlap between personal reign and ancestral tradition.

As a result, the Akwasidae Festival was observed with exceptional grandeur, with all paramountcies within Asanteman in attendance.

Nananom, government officials, diplomats, and thousands of Asanteman citizens have filled the palace forecourt to pay homage.

title: Asantehene Says National House of Chiefs Has No Power to Install Chiefs
author: Bosomtwi-Web
excerpt: The Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, has stated that the National House of Chiefs does not possess the authority to install chiefs, stressing that such powers rest solely with traditional councils.
content:
He made the remarks on Tuesday, May 13, 2026, when the Parliamentary Select Committee on Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs paid a courtesy call on him at the Manhyia Palace.

Addressing members of the committee, the Asantehene cautioned against the politicisation of elections within the National House of Chiefs and urged stakeholders to protect the integrity and independence of the chieftaincy institution.

“What everybody must note is that the House of Chiefs cannot install chiefs. They don’t have that authority. It is the traditional council that does,” he stated.

Otumfuo Osei Tutu II further called on Parliament and relevant state institutions to clearly define the specific responsibilities of the various Houses of Chiefs in matters relating to the enstoolment and recognition of chiefs across the country.

The Asantehene also stressed that he does not depend on government in handling traditional and chieftaincy affairs, explaining that his decisions are guided strictly by the customs, traditions and established practices of the Ashanti Kingdom.

He noted that he has no intention of presenting himself as an autocratic ruler and said he harbours no personal grievances against anyone.

Touching on historical territorial arrangements, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II stated that the Brong Ahafo area historically formed part of Western Ashanti.

According to him, although constitutional administrations over the years introduced changes to territorial governance structures, the historical arrangement has remained unchanged.

The Asantehene further assured the committee that he would continue to uphold truth, fairness and justice in his leadership, while urging the Parliamentary Select Committee to take decisive steps to address the growing challenges confronting the chieftaincy institution in Ghana.

title: Zanetor Rawlings Condemns Xenophobic Attacks in South Africa on AU Day
author: Bosomtwi-Web
excerpt: The Second Deputy President of the Pan-African Parliament and Member of Parliament for Korle Klottey, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, has strongly condemned ongoing xenophobic attacks in South Africa, describing the violence against fellow Africans as a disgrace to the continent’s collective identity and unity.
content:
Speaking during an interview at the flag-raising ceremony marking the 63rd African Union Day held at the State House on Monday, May 25, 2026, Dr Agyeman-Rawlings warned that recurring anti-immigrant violence continues to damage Africa’s global image and weaken confidence in the continent’s leadership.

According to her, the disturbing scenes emerging from South Africa represent a major setback at a time when Africa should be strengthening its geopolitical influence and promoting continental unity.

“The systematic targeting of fellow Africans is a shameful stain on the collective conscience of the continent,” she stated.

### Betraying the Vision of African Unity

African Union Day is commemorated annually on May 25 to celebrate the establishment of the Organisation of African Unity in 1963, which later evolved into the African Union in 2002.

The celebration is aimed at promoting African unity, economic integration, resilience and decolonisation across the continent.

Dr Agyeman-Rawlings argued that the xenophobic attacks directly contradict the ideals of Pan-Africanism and the sacrifices made by Africa’s founding leaders.

She stressed that Africa cannot celebrate institutional progress while citizens from different African countries are allegedly being targeted, displaced and attacked by fellow Africans.

The Korle Klottey MP further urged continental institutions to move beyond symbolic diplomacy and take decisive action to protect human rights and preserve peace across member states.

### Call for Practical Pan-Africanism

Also speaking at the ceremony, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs, James Gyakye Quayson, noted that the principles of Pan-Africanism remain highly relevant to Africa’s modern development agenda.

However, he challenged the African Union to move beyond rhetoric and ideological discussions.

According to him, the continental body must focus on practical interventions that improve human dignity, accelerate economic growth and strengthen unity among African nations.

Mr. Gyakye Quayson stressed that the AU should not exist merely as a political concept discussed in conference rooms but must become a force for real transformation and socioeconomic progress across the continent.

title: Shatta Wale bags two awards at 43rd IRAWMA Awards
author: GNA
excerpt: Ghanaian dancehall artiste Charles Nii Armah Mensah, known as Shatta Wale, has won two awards at the 43rd International Reggae and World Music Awards (IRAWMA) held in Florida over the weekend.
content:
He picked up the Best African Dancehall Entertainer award as well as Concert of the Year for ShattaFest.

In a statement, Shatta Wale’s management expressed appreciation to the organisers and supporters of the awards.

“Management would like to sincerely appreciate the organisers of the IRAWMA awards for the recognition and continuous support for African music on the global stage.

“We also extend our deepest gratitude to fans across the world, especially the Shatta Movement fraternity, for their unwavering support, votes, and dedication throughout the years,” the statement said.

The statement added that the latest wins reaffirm the artiste’s position as one of Africa’s leading musical exports and a prominent figure in global dancehall culture.

The awards bring Shatta Wale’s total haul at the IRAWMA to 11, highlighting his continued presence on the international reggae and dancehall scene.

At last year’s edition, he won three awards: Best African Dancehall Entertainer, Best Music Video for “Killa Ji Mi”, and Best Crossover Song for “Commando” featuring Bounty Killer.

title: EPA Announces Nationwide Ban on Styrofoam Products Effective 2027
author: Bosomtwi Web
excerpt: The Environmental Protection Authority has announced a nationwide ban on the production, importation, distribution, sale and use of polystyrene foam products, commonly known as Styrofoam or takeaway packs, effective January 1, 2027.
content:
The directive follows a policy announcement made by President John Dramani Mahama on June 5, 2025, during World Environment Day celebrations, where he outlined government plans to phase out styrofoam products as part of efforts to address plastic pollution and protect the environment.

In a statement issued on Monday, May 25, 2026, the EPA said the ban will apply to all expanded polystyrene (EPS) foam products used for both commercial and domestic purposes.

These include food packaging containers and takeaway packs, disposable cups and plates, foam packaging used by restaurants and food vendors, as well as foam-based materials used in bedding, insulation and packaging.

The Authority clarified that EPS products used for medical, scientific, laboratory and diagnostic purposes will be exempt, subject to regulatory approval.

According to the EPA, the policy forms part of broader national efforts to improve environmental sanitation, protect public health, reduce plastic pollution and promote sustainable development.

The agency added that the period leading up to enforcement in 2027 will be used for stakeholder engagement, public education and technical consultations across the country.

During this transition phase, the EPA will also intensify compliance monitoring, inspections and enforcement preparedness in collaboration with relevant institutions.

Manufacturers, importers, distributors and users of styrofoam products have been urged to begin shifting toward environmentally friendly, reusable and recyclable alternatives ahead of the ban.

The Authority further stated that it will work with Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies, port authorities, customs officials and industry regulators to ensure effective enforcement once the policy takes full effect.

title: Contracta Construction Lays Off 150 Workers Over Funding Delays on Major Kumasi Projects
author: Bosomtwi Web
excerpt: Contracta Construction UK Ltd., the contractor handling several major infrastructure projects in Kumasi, has laid off about 150 workers following nearly two years of inactivity at project sites due to delayed government payments.
content:
The company is responsible for the Kejetia Phase II Market redevelopment, the Komfo Anokye Maternity and Children’s Block, and the Prempeh I International Airport project.

Speaking to Citi News, the Public Relations and Community Liaison Consultant for the company in Kumasi, Emmanuel Danso, explained that engineers, technicians, and labourers across the three projects were affected as part of cost-cutting measures linked to prolonged financial constraints.

According to him, the company has received only one payment from government since 2024, a situation he said has significantly slowed project execution and forced management to scale down operations.

He added that although the layoffs were unavoidable, all affected workers were fully compensated before being released.

Mr. Danso further revealed that discussions are ongoing between government officials and the company’s directors in Accra to resolve the payment issues and enable work to resume on the projects.

He expressed optimism that the negotiations would lead to the recall of workers and the restart of construction activities.

“Since May 2024, we have received only one payment. So, while negotiations with the government are ongoing, it has become necessary for us to reduce our staff strength… This is not a situation where they are being sent away empty-handed,” he stated.

The development has raised renewed concerns about delays in key infrastructure projects and their broader impact on employment, healthcare delivery, transport infrastructure, and economic activity in Kumasi.
  source: Citi News

title: Editorial: Nana Yaa Akyaa II – A Queen Mother Shaped by Service, Heritage and Duty
author: Bosomtwi Web
excerpt: The enstoolment of Nana Yaa Akyaa II as the 15th Asantehemaa marks the beginning of a significant new chapter in the history of the Asante Kingdom.
content:
Beyond the traditional rites and royal ceremonies lies the remarkable life story of a woman whose journey reflects deep royal heritage, professional accomplishment, compassion for humanity and unwavering commitment to family and community.

[image]https://owgcxvdtkhgowguaufsp.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/article-images/body-1784299025384.jpeg[/image]

Born Odehyie Ama Bonsu, and christened Margaret Siribour, on June 3, 1946, Nana Yaa Akyaa II was born into one of the distinguished royal lineages of Asanteman. She is the second of two children born to Daniel Kwame Bonah Siribour and Odehyie Adwoa Akyaa.

Her royal ancestry is firmly rooted in the history of the Asante Kingdom. Through her mother, she is a granddaughter of Nana Akosua Barnie, who herself was the daughter of Nana Akua Bakoma, the mother of the 14th Asantehene, Otumfuo Sir Osei Agyeman Prempeh II (1931–1970). On her father's side, she traces her lineage to the Juaben royal family through Nana Otuo Siribour I, linking her to two of the most respected royal houses in Asante history.

Growing up at Ahenboboano in Ashanti New Town, Kumasi, Nana Yaa Akyaa II spent her formative years under the care of her mother while maintaining close ties with her father in Konongo during school vacations. Those early experiences exposed her to the values of family, discipline and traditional leadership that would later define her life.

Her educational journey reflected the opportunities available to young women determined to excel during her generation. She attended Government Girls School (Yaa Achiaa Girls School) from 1952 to 1957 before proceeding to Mmofraturo Girls' Boarding School between 1958 and 1961. She later completed her secondary education at St. Louis Girls' Senior High School, graduating in 1966, and subsequently acquired vocational training in typing to broaden her professional skills.

Unlike many traditional leaders whose public lives begin with traditional authority, Nana Yaa Akyaa II first built a distinguished career in the corporate and hospitality sectors. She commenced her working life at Queensway Bookshop in Kumasi, a business owned by her uncle, Barima Kwaku Mensah, a former Chairman of Asante Kotoko Sporting Club.

She later joined Kingsway Stores, then operated by Miller Brothers as part of the Unilever Group, where she worked in the company's import and export business. Following her marriage, she relocated to Accra and continued her career with the company before transitioning into the hospitality industry after the closure of Kingsway Stores.

Working alongside her husband, the late Kwame Afriyie, a respected civil engineer from Ejisu Kwaso and Kumasi Apagyafiem, she helped manage the West End Hotel at Mataheko in Accra. Her entrepreneurial instincts later led her back to Kumasi in the late 1990s, where she successfully established and managed her own multi-purpose business.

Yet perhaps the defining feature of Nana Yaa Akyaa II's life has been her quiet commitment to humanitarian service.

Long before ascending the Kusiamoa Stool, she had earned admiration for supporting vulnerable people within her community. For decades, she has been recognised for feeding the poor, providing shelter to disadvantaged persons and opening her home in Ashanti New Town to those in need. Her philanthropy has never been driven by publicity but by a deeply held belief that leadership begins with service to others.

Her family life has equally been characterised by devotion and resilience. Together with her late husband, she raised three children: the late Barima Osei Afriyie, Barima Kwaku Karikari, and Odehyie Akua Gyamfua.

On July 6, 2026, destiny called once again.

Following careful deliberations within the Asante royal establishment, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II selected her to ascend the Kusiamoa Stool, where she assumed the stool name Nana Yaa Akyaa II, succeeding Nana Konadu Yiadom II as the 15th Asantehemaa.

Her ascension represents more than a transition of traditional authority. It brings to the office of Asantehemaa a woman whose life has been shaped by royal heritage, formal education, professional experience, entrepreneurship and an enduring commitment to social responsibility.

The institution of the Asantehemaa has historically played a pivotal role in governance, mediation, cultural preservation, women's empowerment and the welfare of the Asante people. It is a position that demands wisdom, compassion, diplomacy and moral authority.

Nana Yaa Akyaa II assumes that responsibility at a time when traditional leadership continues to complement national development through education, culture, peacebuilding and social cohesion.

Her life story offers a portrait of a Queen Mother prepared not only by birth but also by experience. It is a journey that reflects the enduring values of humility, service, resilience and duty—qualities that have long defined the great women of Asanteman.

As she begins her reign, many across the kingdom will look to her to uphold the rich traditions of the Golden Stool while inspiring a new generation through leadership rooted in compassion, wisdom and unwavering commitment to the welfare of her people.

title: Otumfuo Calls for Integrity, Enterprise and Ethical Leadership to Transform Ghana
author: Bosomtwi-Web
excerpt: The Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, has called on Ghanaians to shift national focus from political rhetoric to enterprise, integrity and ethical leadership as the country approaches its seventh decade of independence.
content:
Speaking at the Ghana Business Leaders’ Conclave held at the University of Professional Studies, Accra on May 15, 2026, under the theme “Leading With Integrity: Negotiation, Mediation and Ethical Governance for Business Sustainability,” the Asantehene said Ghana’s transformation depends largely on integrity-driven leadership.

According to him, business without integrity is dangerous, leadership without humility is arrogance, and prosperity without ethics is fragile.

“Let this conclave send forth leaders who understand that negotiation is not manipulation, mediation is not weakness, governance is not bureaucracy, and business is not greed,” he stated.

Otumfuo expressed optimism that the conclave would produce a new generation of leaders committed to building enterprises, resolving disputes, creating jobs, honouring contracts, protecting the environment and serving the nation.

“If we do this, then the next decade will not be another decade of lamentation. It will be a decade of enterprise. It will be a decade of ethical leadership. It will be a decade of builders,” he added.

### Ghana’s Historic Role

Reviewing Ghana’s place in African and global history, the Asantehene noted that the country played a critical role in the continent’s liberation struggles.

“From Algeria to Angola, Mozambique to Zimbabwe, from the struggle against colonial domination to the collapse of apartheid in South Africa, the hand of Ghana was ever present, ever firm, and ever critical,” he said.

He also highlighted the global contributions of distinguished Ghanaians including Kofi Annan, Robert Gardiner, Kenneth Dadzie, and Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey.

### Concern Over Economic Hardship

Despite Ghana’s historic achievements, Otumfuo lamented that the promises of independence have not translated into prosperity for many citizens.

“There is no truer measure of our national progress than the state of our economy. It is the economy that determines whether we are able to provide food for the table, shelter for families, clothes for children, education for our people, healthcare for our communities, and safety for our homes,” he said.

The Asantehene identified excessive political partisanship as one of the major causes of Ghana’s stagnation, arguing that party loyalty has too often taken precedence over national interest.

“Politics has clouded those decades because allegiance to party has too often been stronger than allegiance to the state,” he stated.

He further observed that the country had spent too much time celebrating politicians while neglecting entrepreneurs, innovators and hardworking citizens whose efforts drive economic growth.

### ‘Ghana Must Become a Nation of Builders’

Otumfuo Osei Tutu II stressed that Ghana must move beyond slogans and promises toward practical nation-building and productivity.

“After almost 70 years, the lesson is clear. We have had enough of the talk. Ghana must now become a nation of builders,” he declared.

“We must move from political rhetoric to building businesses. We must move from slogans to production. We must move from lamentation to enterprise. We must move from dependency to value creation.”

He said the coming decade must be dedicated to building a resilient, ethical and sustainable economy driven by innovation, discipline, sacrifice and hard work.

According to him, while political leaders have a responsibility to provide sound policies and stability, citizens, professionals, entrepreneurs and institutions must also embrace innovation and value creation.

### Trust Deficit in Leadership

The Asantehene also expressed concern over what he described as a growing trust deficit in leadership across the country.

“Every four or eight years, we welcome leaders with great hope, yet too often loyalty is short-lived, trust is fragile, and our heroes soon end up in the depths of disappointment,” he said.

He warned that declining trust now extends beyond politics into businesses, schools, boardrooms and homes, posing a threat to national cohesion and development.

“Democracy requires elections, but nation-building requires trust. Democracy changes government, but trust sustains societies,” he noted.

### Integrity as the Foundation of Leadership

Otumfuo defined integrity as the true test of character and leadership.

“It is how a person behaves when nobody is watching. It is how a leader acts when power is in his hands. It is how a manager decides when profit is at stake. It is how a country behaves when convenience tempts it away from truth,” he said.

Drawing from his experience in conflict resolution within Asanteman and beyond, he noted that fairness, patience, honesty and perseverance are essential virtues in both governance and business.

“A negotiator without integrity manipulates. A mediator without fairness destroys trust,” he cautioned.

### Inspiration from UPSA Founder

The Asantehene also recounted the story of Nana Opoku Ampoma, founder of what later became UPSA, praising his vision and determination.

“He did not sit waiting for government. He did not wail over the difficulty but asked himself what he could do for the nation,” Otumfuo said.

“What began as a dream in difficult circumstances has today become UPSA. His success resulted from the application of integrity.”

### Message to Students

Addressing students at the conclave, Otumfuo urged them to prioritise character over academic qualifications.

“When that day comes, Ghana will not only ask what degree you obtained, but what kind of person you became,” he said.

He encouraged the younger generation to reject corruption, environmental destruction and divisive politics, while embracing ethical leadership, discipline, service and responsibility.

“You must be modern, rooted and ambitious but ethical, confident, humble, successful, and then responsible,” the Asantehene concluded.

title: Court of Appeal restores license of GN Savings and Loans
author: Graphic Online
excerpt: The Court of Appeal has by a unanimous decision restored the license of GN Savings and Loans Company Limited.
content:
That was after a three-member panel of the second-highest court quashed the decision of the High Court, which upheld the revocation of the license on the grounds that the decision to revoke the license was unfair and unreasonable.

By the judgment, both the decision to revoke the license and the High Court decision to uphold same has been quashed.

The court ordered the receiver should also hand over possession, management and control of the assets and other activities to shareholders of the company.

Background 


On January 4, 2019, GN Bank Limited was reclassified as a savings and loans company and consequently renamed GN Savings and Loans Company Limited.

Seven months later, on August 16, 2019, the BoG, then under the leadership of Dr Ernest Addison, revoked the operating licence of GN Savings and Loans Company Limited and appointed Eric Nana Nipah as Receiver as part of the banking sector clean-up exercise.

The same month, Groupe Nduom, owners of GN Savings and Loans Company Limited, led by Dr Papa Kwesi Nduom, challenged the revocation of the licence in the High Court in Accra.

On January 24, 2024, Justice Addo upheld the revocation of the licence.


It is this judgment of the High Court which owners of GN Savings and Loans Company Limited, led by Dr Papa Kwesi Nduom, challenged that has been quashed.

title: Two Chinese Nationals Arrested in Illegal Mining Raid Along Dankai River
author: Bosomtwi-Web
excerpt: Two Chinese nationals have been arrested following a joint pre-dawn operation by the National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat and the Blue Water Guards after authorities uncovered an illegal mining enclave where portions of the Dankai River had allegedly been blocked and diverted.
content:
The operation took place at Sanfo Adiam in the Amansie East District between 4:00 a.m. and 7:00 a.m. on Sunday, May 24, 2026.

According to the task force, the raid followed credible intelligence regarding organised galamsey activities along the Dankai River corridor.

Officials said operatives moved from their Manso Adubia base under the cover of darkness in an effort to reach the mining sites before operators could flee.

The two suspects, identified as Lu Honggeng, 53, and Nong Zisun, 41, reportedly attempted to escape during the operation but were chased and apprehended by the task force.

Authorities alleged that the suspects and their associates had blocked and redirected sections of the Dankai River into an artificial dam to supply water for mining activities.

NAIMOS described the diversion of the river as a serious environmental violation that threatens the river’s natural flow and communities that rely on it downstream.

Officials further indicated that the operation successfully disrupted the illegal damming and diversion activities along the river.

The arrested individuals have since been transferred to the NAIMOS Secretariat in Accra for further investigations and are expected to be handed over to the Ghana Immigration Service.

The Secretariat also reiterated its commitment to sustaining anti-galamsey operations in Amansie East and other affected areas until polluted and damaged rivers are restored.

NAIMOS warned illegal miners to desist from activities that continue to destroy Ghana’s water bodies and forest reserves.

title: Bright Simons Warns NITA Bill Could Create Overreach in Ghana’s Digital Sector
author: Citinewsroom
excerpt: One of Ghana’s veteran business journalists, now based in New York, reached out and asked if I have been following the NITA bill debate. Sadly, I hadn’t. Too much going on.Ghana travel guide
content:
He pressed, subtly but firmly, so I did.

I appreciate the ambition of the current management at the Ministry. I am sure they want their names in neon above Black Star Square. But there is a serious katanomic odour blowing from the bill they are promoting.

They would do well to assemble a group of truly independent tech folks from the ICT chamber, not just a bunch of their friends, listen hard, talk less, and take the advice. If they did, they would gut that manuscript and return to the drawing board.

Here is why, based on my quick take on the bill.

Bottom line

The Ministry of Communications, Digital Technology, & Innovations (MOC) does not merely appear to be proposing to “license IT professionals.”

The draft NITA Bill is much bigger. The plan is to convert NITA from a coordinating ICT agency into a broad digital-sector regulator with powers over ICT infrastructure, cloud, SaaS, digital platforms, public-sector technology procurement, professional certification, business premises, mergers, ownership, standards, audits, sanctions, and even the structure of government digital infrastructure. It is a wholesale revamp.


No one would have quarrelled with the bill if it had focused on the big problems in the sector: public sector procurement indiscipline and a lack of incentives for R&D and support for local tech innovations.

Ghana certainly needs improved standards and practices in digital assurance, interoperability, and accountability for critical systems (already captured in the “critical infrastructure” policy).

The katanomics arise when instead of learning from national mistakes and proposing workable solutions, one jumps the process to venture into a whole range of areas where the country absolutely lack policy experience.

1. MOC’s Proposals

The draft/consultation bill proposes as follows:

A stronger NITA “Authority”

The Bill would establish NITA as a regulatory authority for ICT and digital services, with objects including regulation, coordination, promotion, standards, licensing, certification, interoperability, digital innovation, and public-sector ICT personnel management.

Mandatory licensing of ICT business activity

Section 35 (the bombshell that has sparked so much controversy). It says no person may engage in business or a related activity in the ICT sector unless granted a licence. It expressly includes installation of ICT infrastructure, development or provision of ICT products and services, and activities requiring licensing or certification. Doing any of these without a license could get one jailed, or at best fined.

Who is to be licensed?

Section 36 lists categories such as public/commercial ICT infrastructure, cloud hosting, SaaS providers, government digital services partnerships, national digital platform operators, data centre operators, and any other category the Authority later determines.

Citizen-only ownership qualification

Section 37 says a licence applicant must be an adult Ghanaian citizen, or a company/partnership/association/body “wholly owned by a citizen.” Essentially, it would now be illegal to engage remote experts to work on a system deployed in Ghana. Essentially, half the whiz kids in Silicon Valley would have been ineligible to build their genius gizmos had America had a law like this.

Certification of ICT professionals

Section 46 says a person shall not be appointed as an ICT professional in a public or private institution unless certified by the Authority, and that NITA shall determine the criteria and procedure. (Funnily, this contradicts the definitions section where “certified professional” is confined to the public sector.)

Closure, seizure, suspension and enforcement powers


NITA could close premises or facilities, seize ICT products/equipment, suspend business, revoke licences, and impose administrative penalties in specified circumstances.

M&A and business-structure control

 Section 49 appears to require NITA approval before sale, transfer, merger, amalgamation, or alteration of the nature of an ICT service provider’s business.

There are also some less controversial proposals about setting up a special purpose national e-government vehicle, promoting transparency and interoperability, and preventing vendor lock-in.

Let’s focus, however, on the areas of the Bill that have rankled so many ICT professionals and would clearly not have seen the light of the day if the Ministry bosses had done any serious sounding beyond their clique.

2. What do they mean by “ICT professional” anyway?

“IT/ICT professional” is not like “nurse,” “electrician,” “lawyer,” “chartered accountant,” or “professional engineer.” Those occupations usually have a more defined body of practice, recognised training path, public-risk rationale, and a reserved act or protected title.

“ICT” and “IT” are very loose umbrella terms. International occupational systems do not treat ICT as one unified profession. The International Standard Classification of Occupations classifies jobs by skill level and specialisation, not by one vague “IT professional” identity.


Eurostat and O*NET both list many distinct computer and mathematical occupations within that bracket: software developers, network architects, cybersecurity analysts, database administrators, web developers, data scientists, support specialists, QA testers, IT project managers, and many more.

Is the government of Ghana going to insist on licensing every single person in Ghana who builds a website, uses Microsoft Power BI to create some charts for a company, or deploys mermaid to craft some flyers for an event organiser?Ghana travel guide

The whole idea is totally ridiculous.

A more sensible approach would be to pry open the ICT chest open and only target the most critical functions. Example:

Critical Public Digital Infrastructure management (with a clear and rigorous process properly defined as to how any system gets to be elevated to that status to begin with);
Financial services cybersecurity auditing;
Tier II & III datacenter operations;
Public hospital digital health network administration;
Public ERP procurement readiness certtification.
The bill could then have said that for those functions, licensed professionals are required. The licensing regime would then have been constructed in an industry-led fashion much like we have in leading accounting jurisdictions. Frankly, the civil service is the last place to situate licensing for a dynamic sector like ICT.

More importantly, under no circumstances should any government aspire to poke its long nose into stuff like “writing code,” “installing a router,” “maintaining a school website,” “handling some graphic design,” “being a product manager at a food delivery company,” “using AI to generate a UI for a service,” or “working in an IT department of a small law firm.” The risks are not national-scale and employers should be left to manage their own personnel validation.

3. Ghanaian laws already provide some protection

A standard feature of Katanomics is to pile laws upon laws without much effort being spent on reviewing how the current laws are performing, why gaps, if any, have formed, and what the lessons really teach.

The Cybersecurity Act creates a targeted licensing/accreditation regime for cybersecurity service providers, establishments, professionals and practitioners. That makes sense because cybersecurity services can create high systemic risk, and the Act contains a specific institutional mandate around cyber protection. If that has not stopped fraud in banks and telcos, there is a need to enhance our understanding and respond accordingly.


The Data Protection Act regulates controllers and processors of personal data, requires registration, imposes security obligations, requires written processor arrangements, and provides breach-notification duties. If the Data Protection Commission is only taken fees and isn’t really measuring up, the right approach is to fix it.

The Engineering Council could decide to create top-tier categories for “software engineering,” as well as hardware and electronic engineering if it aims to elevate the field. It already has the pedigree and legal infrastructure to proceed if it deems the time right.

4. But don’t other countries already do this?

Well, some have tried but the lessons are worth taking.

Nigeria, for instance. The Computer Professionals Registration Council of Nigeria was created under a 1993 law and has a broad mandate over persons and organisations providing computing professional services.

The arrangement in Nigeria has gone nowhere. The country still has a huge informal and startup-driven tech sector. In practice, broad computing-profession regulation tends to become procurement gatekeeping, dues, professional conferences, anti-“quackery” rhetoric, and credential signalling. It has generated nothing of clear value to the sector.

Canada shows a narrower and more legally coherent model. Engineering regulators restrict titles such as “software engineer,” “computer engineer,” and “firmware engineer” where those titles imply professional engineering. But even there, regulators recognise that not all software development is software engineering. The Canadian fights over “software engineer” titles show how hard it is to map old professional-engineering concepts onto modern tech labour markets.


The United States tried a software-engineering professional-engineer exam pathway. The software engineering PE exam was first offered in 2013 and discontinued after 2019 because candidate numbers were too low.

Almost everywhere else, the approach has been to rely more on voluntary professional bodies, chartered status, competence frameworks, sector standards, procurement rules, data protection, cyber regulation, product regulation, and critical-infrastructure obligations. In many of these contexts and jurisdictions, industry associations take the lead.

5. It can get absurd pretty quickly

Meanwhile, AI has thrown a wrench into the whole wheel of what “IT work” even means today. m

In the pre-AI world, one might imagine a recognisable “software developer” writing code manually. In the AI world, a founder describes an app to a model, a non-technical employee uses AI to build an internal workflow, a designer generates front-end code, a business analyst deploys automations, and a cloud platform assembles infrastructure through templates. Who is the “ICT professional” here? The geography graduate with a few hours on reddit and stackoverflow under her belt typing out prompts? The AI tool vendor? The person who clicks deploy? The person who reviews the code? The company using the system?

A licensing regime based on “professional identity” will clash with AI-generated work because AI diffuses technical production across the entire economy. The more powerful AI gets, the less realistic it becomes to require every producer of digital functionality to hold a state-issued ICT license. Once again, if the Ministry had engaged beyond their small clique, everyone would have told them.

6. Hardware, networking and informality

On the physical device and network level, the absurdity start to get out of hand.

Ghana’s ICT economy is not made up of just software startups. It includes laptop repairers, phone technicians, CCTV installers, router vendors, fibre/cabling contractors, school computer-lab maintainers, POS support agents, small network installers, market traders selling peripherals, informal refurbished-device dealers, cybercafé operators, church/media livestream technicians, and thousands of small businesses that keep digital life functioning. All these people are using ICT and making a living in the ICT-enabled economy.Ghana travel guide

If enforced aggressively, the scheme could:

raise the cost of basic repairs and installations;
push informal technicians further underground;
create opportunities for inspectors and middlemen to extract bribes;
make small businesses operate through “certified” fronts;
reduce access to affordable hardware support in rural and low-income areas;
increase e-waste if repair markets are chilled;
make public-sector maintenance more expensive by reducing the pool of eligible providers.
It is a whole mess, and must be reined in before it transmutes from panic to catastrophe.

7. And the MESS doesn’t end there

The citizen-only ownership clause is potentially devastating. A Ghanaian startup with foreign VC, non-citizen co-founders, regional holding structures, offshore investors, or employee stock held by non-citizens may struggle if licensed ICT activity requires wholly citizen ownership. This may be more economically explosive than the “IT professionals” headline.

NITA, the Cyber Security Authority, Data Protection Commission, National Communications Authority, Bank of Ghana, Ghana Standards Authority, Public Procurement Authority, GIPC, Engineering Council, and sector regulators may all touch the same digital product. A fintech, for example, could face payment regulation, data protection registration, cybersecurity obligations, NITA licensing, cloud/data-centre requirements, and public procurement rules. The cost of doing business is already too high. Don’t make it worse!


The Bill includes criminal offences, administrative penalties, licence suspension, business prohibition, closure, seizure, and penalties for negligent cybersecurity breaches or false certification claims. Some of that is justified for critical misconduct, but excessive criminalisation can chill innovation and incident reporting.

Now imagine:

A small NGO building a data-collection app could be treated as developing/providing an ICT product.

A small periurban school near Techiman appointing a self-taught but competent ICT teacher or network administrator could run into the Section 46 certification requirement if “ICT professional” is read broadly.

A startup adding cloud hosting, AI features, or platform functionality might need to ask whether it has changed the “nature” of its ICT business and needs approval.

A Ghanaian founder could be treated less favourably after raising foreign investment than before raising it.

An AI-assisted non-programmer could produce useful code, while a formally certified but incompetent person is legally privileged.

Even worse:

The merger/alteration approval clause is dangerous because it turns ordinary corporate switches into a whole regulatory fanfare. Startup pivots, acquisitions, restructurings and investment rounds depend on speed and certainty.

More licensing layers are likely to lead to slower product launches, especially in already tough fields like fintech. Think also about the higher legal costs, and more uncertainty for firms already dealing with Bank of Ghana, data protection, cybersecurity and AML obligations.

Paradoxically, overregulation can weaken cybersecurity. Small operators may avoid registration, breach reporting, or formal contracts because contact with the regulator feels dangerous.

Conversely, employers may over-apply the law and require NITA certification for analysts, IT support, product managers, data officers, website administrators, and junior developers, even where the legal risk is unclear.


Moreover, Ghana participates in regional and continental liberalisation frameworks, including ECOWAS free movement/establishment principles and AfCFTA services liberalisation. A broad citizen-only ICT licensing scheme may create avoidable trade and investment friction, even if Ghana retains policy space to regulate for legitimate objectives.Ghana travel guide

It is true that the Bill creates an appeals tribunal, but the tribunal is appointed through ministerial processes and funded through the NITA’s funds. Appeals to the Court of Appeal, on the other hand, are limited to points of law. That may be insufficient for a regime with such heavy commercial consequences.

9. A better law might look something like this

The Bill should be rewritten around regulated activities, not “IT professionals.”

The following quick fixes would be a good start:

Replace the broad Section 35 ban with a schedule of licensable high-risk ICT activities: public & sensitive commercial digital infrastructure, critical data centres, public cloud for government/critical sectors, critical SaaS for public services, cybersecurity-sensitive operations, and national platform operators.
Rewrite Section 46 so certification applies only to defined risk roles: public-sector chief information/security officers, critical infrastructure administrators, certified ICT auditors, digital identity administrators, public procurement sign-off professionals, and cybersecurity-sensitive roles. For everyone else, use voluntary certification or title protection.
Add exemptions for employees doing internal work, students, hobbyists, open-source contributors, micro repairers, ordinary retail sales, internal IT departments, low-risk website/app development, and small businesses below clear thresholds.
Remove or radically narrow the citizen-only ownership rule. Use public-procurement preferences, local-capacity requirements, security vetting for sensitive contracts, and Ghanaian participation incentives instead of a blanket nationality-based ownership restriction.
Limit transaction approvals to changes of control of high-risk licensees. Do not require approval for ordinary pivots, product changes, share issuances, acquisitions outside sensitive categories, or internal restructuring.
Create a lead-regulator rule. If the CSA, DPC, NCA, Bank of Ghana or another regulator already licenses the core risk, NITA should coordinate through memoranda and joint standards, rather than duplicating permissions.
Hardwire the due process in. The Bill should require that there should be published criteria, fee caps, timelines, deemed approvals where appropriate, written reasons, appeal stays except in emergencies, warrant requirements for seizure except imminent-risk cases, and compensation for wrongful closure.
Build an AI-specific assurance layer. Require secure development practices, AI-use documentation, human review for high-risk systems, logging, testing, model/data governance, incident reporting and audit trails. Avoid creating an “outmoded at birth” bill because of a failure to take AI into account.
Be sensitive to the informal economy. Ensure long transition periods, recognition of prior learning, apprenticeship routes, low-cost micro-certification, mobile registration, district-level support, and no criminal enforcement for low-risk actors during transition.
Require a regulatory impact assessment before commencement. The government should publish expected costs, affected occupations, SME effects, competition analysis, trade implications, institutional overlaps, enforcement budget, and anti-corruption safeguards.Conclusion: the Ministry is off the bar but they can have another go
A careful NITA law could be one of Ghana’s most anti-katanomic and groundbreaking digital economy reforms. Especially if it focuses on fixing wasteful, opaque, and pooly thought through public ICT procurement.

But a careless version could become a massive burden on the heads of a struggling, still nascent, technology sector. The draft bill tilts more to the latter than the former.

The MOC should get off its high horse while there is still time, abandon the bill in its current form, return to the drawing board, and come back with something more aligned with modern realities.

About the Author 

Bright Simons is a Ghanaian technologist, social innovator, entrepreneur, writer, social and political commentator. He is the vice-president, in charge of research at IMANI Centre for Policy and Education. He is also the founder and president of mPedigree.

title: Government to Allocate Additional Minerals Fund Support for Roads in Mining Communities
author: Bosomtwi Web
excerpt: The Ashanti Regional Minister, Frank Amoakohene, has announced that government will provide additional funding from the Minerals Development Fund to improve road infrastructure in mining communities across the Ashanti Region.
content:
Dr. Amoakohene disclosed this during a working visit to Obuasi West Municipal and Obuasi East Municipal, where he inspected ongoing government and District Assemblies Common Fund (DACF) projects alongside the Chief Director of the Ashanti Regional Coordinating Council, Michael Owusu Amoako.

According to the Regional Minister, mining communities will benefit from targeted road infrastructure support under the Minerals Fund in addition to existing allocations made to Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies.

“As mining areas, the government has taken a decision to make additional allocations under the Minerals Fund specifically to cater for roads in mining communities. This is in addition to 10km of roads allocated to each MMDA,” he stated.

Dr. Amoakohene assured residents that government remains committed to addressing the deteriorating road conditions in mining areas through deliberate and sustained interventions.

During the visit, the Regional Minister also interacted with staff of both assemblies and paid courtesy calls on traditional authorities in the area together with the Municipal Chief Executives.

The MCEs briefed the Minister on several ongoing development projects within their respective municipalities.

Describing the Obuasi enclave as strategically important to government, Dr. Amoakohene stressed the need for regular field inspections to monitor projects and assess progress on the ground.

He commended the Municipal Chief Executives, Faustilove Appiah Kannin of Obuasi West and William Kofi Adzowu of Obuasi East, as well as staff of the assemblies, for their dedication and performance in executing development projects.

The Regional Minister further reaffirmed government’s commitment to decentralised development, revealing that 80 percent of the DACF has already been disbursed to Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies with clear expenditure guidelines.

He added that government has also made provisions for the development of markets to support the implementation of the 24-hour economy initiative.

The working visit forms part of efforts by the Regional Minister to promote accountability and accelerate development projects across the Ashanti Region.

title: Ghana Music Awards-USA unveils 2026 nominees in Kumasi
author: Source: Joy Entertainment
excerpt: The Ghana Music Awards USA (GMA-USA) has officially unveiled nominees for its 2026 awards, with a vibrant ceremony held at The Octopus, Kumasi City Mall, on Thursday, April 30, 2026.
content:
The event drew artistes, industry stakeholders and music lovers, reflecting the growing influence of Ghanaian music both locally and internationally. This year’s scheme recognises talent across 35 categories, with 24 dedicated to US-based Ghanaian acts and 11 focused on artistes in Ghana. The structure reinforces GMA-USA’s aim of bridging Ghana’s home industry with its diaspora in the United States.

Speaking at the event, organisers stressed the importance of celebrating Ghanaian music on a global stage. Dennis Boafo, also known as Don D, CEO of Ghana Music Awards USA, said:
“We are proud to provide a platform that acknowledges the outstanding achievements of artists both in Ghana and the US. This dual focus strengthens the connection between our communities and showcases the diversity of Ghanaian music to the world.”

The night featured performances from Kumasi-based artistes including Adom Kiki and Xheila, offering a glimpse of the talent set to compete at the main ceremony later this year. The event also created opportunities for networking among artistes, promoters and stakeholders, further encouraging collaboration within the global Ghanaian music community.
As anticipation builds towards the awards night, fans and industry watchers are keen to see which artistes will emerge winners, with GMA-USA continuing to spotlight Ghanaian talent on the world stage.
